title: The first week: loved sinner
hookLine: the Exercises begin with honest sorrow held by mercy

cards: Ignatius divides his Spiritual Exercises into weeks. A week, in his book, isn't seven days. He says plainly that some people will take longer over a week and some shorter, depending on what they're given.

A week is a stage, a movement of the heart, and the first is the hard one. Ignatius asks the person praying to look honestly at sin: the angels' sin, Adam and Eve's, and then their own. That sounds grim.
But the way he sets it up, the looking never happens alone.

teach.b: Ignatius doesn't ask anyone to stare at their failures in an empty room. He asks them to do it standing before Christ on the cross, and to talk with him the way one friend talks to another, asking three plain questions.

teach.h: WHAT HAVE I DONE, AM DOING, OUGHT I TO DO?
teach.b: What have I done for Christ? What am I doing for Christ? What ought I to do for Christ?
That's the frame of the whole week. The sorrow is real; Ignatius even asks for the grace of tears. But it's sorrow in front of one who, Christians say, already died for the one praying.
Paul puts it this way: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." While we were yet sinners. Not after we cleaned up.
Somewhere in the first week, Ignatius has the person praying break into wonder. Why didn't the earth swallow me?
Why have the sun and the stars, the fruits and the animals, the angels and the saints, all gone on holding me up? In Ignatius's telling, the answer is mercy, there the whole time.
Jesus's story of the son who comes home has the picture: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him."
The father runs before the son can say a word of his speech. That's the first week: a loved sinner, both words true at once.
Look back over this week of going inward, from Teresa's castle to Ignatius's freedom, and it ends here: in his picture, the one who comes home finds the door already open.

how: In the Spiritual Exercises, whether in a long silent retreat or in daily life with a guide, the first week is spent praying over sin and God's mercy, often ending in a conversation with Christ on the cross and, for Catholics, sometimes in confession.

games.q: you're in the first week, looking honestly at your own failures. Ignatius has you stand before Christ on the cross. what do you do?
o: talk with him as a friend and ask what you've done, are doing, and ought to do for him.
promise to fix everything before you come back.
games.why: Ignatius ends the meditation with a conversation, as one friend speaks to another, and three questions. sorrow, held in a relationship.

practice: Let one thing you've done wrong come to mind, something real but not the heaviest thing you carry; this is two minutes, not a lifetime.
Name it plainly, without excuses and without piling on, and imagine it held, not thrown back at you.
If you pray, bring it before Christ on the cross and ask Ignatius's three questions; if you don't, hold it next to the picture of a father running down a road.

wordCard.voice: The first week. The opening stage of Ignatius's Exercises: honest sorrow for sin, held in front of a mercy that came first.

carryVoice: Your line: loved, as I am. Honest sorrow and mercy, held together at once. See you tomorrow.
